agreement_rule.two_or_more_bands_apart: anchor ambiguity - reword, do not average

gates: Neither pole is better. Every dimension runs between two legitimate cultures. “Directed” is not worse than “self-directed.” If you catch yourself scoring toward the pole you personally prefer, stop — that is bias, not signal.

Score the company as it is, not as you would like it. You are describing a culture, not grading it. Aspirational careers-page copy is weak evidence; how people describe daily reality is strong evidence.
Kill the halo. A well-liked brand tends to drag every score toward “good.” Score each dimension only from evidence about that dimension.

Evidence over gut. If you cannot point to a line in the packet that supports the number, lower your confidence. A guess dressed as a 0.9 poisons the ground truth more than an honest 0.5 at low confidence.
Stale culture is wrong culture. Prefer recent evidence. Where the packet flags an evidence-age problem, let it lower your confidence.
Do not search for anything in this packet. If you recognise the company, that is expected and is not a failure — tick the recognition box and keep scoring from the evidence in front of you.

confidence_bands.label: High
confidence_bands.text: Multiple corroborating sources of different types all point the same way.

confidence_bands.label: Medium
confidence_bands.text: Some real evidence but from one source type, or sources partly conflict. A defensible read, not a certain one.

confidence_bands.label: Low
confidence_bands.text: Thin or indirect evidence — a single ambiguous signal. You can defend a direction, but only weakly.

confidence_bands.label: Very low
confidence_bands.text: Almost nothing in the packet bears on this dimension. You are close to guessing.

dimensions.name: Autonomy
dimensions.measures: How much latitude individuals have to set their own approach, priorities and decisions, vs. following assigned direction, defined process and approval chains.
dimensions.where_to_look: Job-post verbs (“execute against the roadmap” vs. “own your domain end-to-end”), number of approval layers, presence of detailed SOP/process docs, review mentions of micromanagement vs. freedom, IC decision rights, remote-trust language.
dimensions.keep_distinct: Not the same as Collaboration. A person can be highly self-directed AND work collectively. Autonomy is about who decides the how; Collaboration is about alone vs. together — score meeting and pairing density there, never here. Not the same as Innovation either: a prescribed method can produce novel work and a self-directed team can spend all its time optimizing.

bands.text: Work is assigned and specified top-down. Most decisions need sign-off. Postings stress “follow established processes,” reviews cite micromanagement or rigid procedure.
Manager sets direction and priorities; individual chooses tactics inside clear guardrails. Some latitude, but the frame is given.
Direction set at team level, individuals pick the how within it. No strong signal either way, or genuinely balanced.
ICs own outcomes and choose their approach with light approval. “Ownership,” results-over-process language present.
Individuals set their own priorities and methods with minimal approval. High-trust, flat decision rights pervade the evidence.

dimensions.name: Pace
dimensions.measures: The tempo and intensity of work — deliberate, sustainable cadence vs. rapid, high-urgency, quick-turnaround.
dimensions.where_to_look: “Fast-paced” in postings, release/ship frequency, deadline and crunch culture, review mentions of hours/intensity/burnout vs. calm, on-call expectations.
dimensions.keep_distinct: Not the same as Innovation. A company can move fast while only optimizing, or invent slowly. Pace is tempo; Innovation is novelty.

bands.text: Deliberate cadence, long planning horizons, stability and quality emphasis. Reviews describe a calm, sustainable pace.
Generally measured tempo with occasional pushes. Deadlines exist but rarely dominate.
Ordinary business tempo — some crunch, some calm. No dominant signal.
Regular urgency, frequent releases, tight-ish timelines. Energy is up but not relentless.
“Move fast,” rapid iteration, aggressive deadlines. Reviews cite long hours, intensity or hypergrowth.

dimensions.name: Collaboration
dimensions.measures: How work actually gets produced — individual, heads-down ownership vs. group, cross-functional, in-the-room problem-solving.
dimensions.where_to_look: Team structure (pods/squads vs. single-threaded owners), meeting and pairing culture, open-plan vs. deep-work norms, “we win together” vs. “heads-down, protect your focus time” language, async-written vs. sync-group.
dimensions.keep_distinct:
Not the same as Autonomy. Collective teams can still hand individuals full ownership of the how. Score meeting and team density here, decision rights under Autonomy.

Not the same as Feedback. This was the single most-confused pair in round 1 (9 shared passages, more than any other, and unguarded until now). Warmth and quality of working relationships -- "good team," "supportive coworkers," "people feel comfortable raising concerns" -- are weak Collaboration signals about how much people work together, and are NOT Feedback signals at all. Score HOW MUCH joint work happens here. Score how critique is delivered under Feedback, and only when the evidence actually describes critique.

bands.text: Heads-down solo production is the norm. Very low meeting load, little or no pairing, written async updates in place of live working sessions.
Work is produced alone and brought together at periodic syncs. Meetings are status and handoff, not joint problem-solving.
Balanced individual and group work; no dominant mode.
Cross-functional teamwork common, meetings frequent, decisions shared.
Heavy pairing, meeting and consensus culture, cross-functional pods, “we win together” throughout.

dimensions.name: Feedback Culture
dimensions.measures: How performance feedback flows — occasional and softened vs. frequent, direct and unfiltered.
dimensions.where_to_look: Explicit description of HOW critique is delivered (direct/blunt vs. softened/diplomatic) and HOW OFTEN performance is discussed (frequent 1:1s or check-ins vs. only an annual review, or no formal cycle mentioned at all). "Radical candor," "direct communication," specific review-cycle cadence, and explicit conflict/debate norms are on-axis. General statements about support, recognition, mentorship, career growth, or team friendliness are NOT on-axis even when they use the word "feedback" -- check whether the quote actually describes delivery style or frequency, not just whether it uses feedback-adjacent vocabulary.
dimensions.keep_distinct:
Score the delivery style and frequency of critique specifically -- not whether feedback is "nice," and not general workplace supportiveness. Recognition, appreciation, psychological safety, anti-retaliation policies, mentorship programs, career-development support, and "we care about our people" language are NOT feedback signals.

WARMTH IS ORTHOGONAL TO THIS AXIS AND APPEARS AT BOTH POLES. A caring company may give feedback constantly and bluntly; a cold one may give it rarely and vaguely. Supportive-sounding evidence is not low-band evidence -- it is not evidence on this axis at all. Do not let it pull a score toward either end.

Cross-dimension leaks observed in round 1, in order of how often they occurred:
- COLLABORATION is the most frequent collision (9 shared passages across raters, the highest of any pair, and it had no guardrail in v1 or in the first v3 draft). How often people talk to each other, how good the working relationships are, and whether the team is pleasant to be in are Collaboration (team density) or nothing -- not Feedback. "Comfortable coming forward with questions or concerns," "friendly vibe, good team, good supervisor," "diverse voices and disciplines intersect" were all filed under BOTH dimensions by the same rater. Feedback needs a statement about CRITIQUE: how bluntly it is delivered, or how often.
- AUTONOMY: "acts on instinct, not instruction" is Autonomy, not Feedback.
- PACE: response-time expectations ("no one expected to respond immediately") and work-cadence rituals (a weekly "housekeeping" or catch-up day) are Pace, not Feedback, even when they involve people talking to each other regularly.

bands.text: Feedback is occasional and softened. Critique, when it comes, is cushioned or indirect, and open disagreement is rare in the evidence.
Feedback arrives mainly on a fixed cycle and is delivered diplomatically. Directness is the exception.
Normal mix of scheduled and ad-hoc feedback, moderate directness.
Frequent, fairly direct feedback; debate is normal; thicker skin helps.
Radical candor, constant unfiltered input, “we tell it straight,” critique and debate are the default.

dimensions.name: Innovation Stance
dimensions.measures: Where the work sits on the create-vs-refine axis — improving and scaling what exists vs. inventing what does not exist yet.
dimensions.where_to_look: R&D emphasis, “0-to-1” vs. “scale what works” language, how much of the roadmap is new capability vs. improvement of shipped capability, tolerance for failed bets. Ignore process rigidity here — a documented, tightly-governed process says nothing about whether the output is novel, and belongs under Autonomy.
dimensions.keep_distinct: Not the same as Pace. Optimizing can be frantic; inventing can be slow. Score novelty of the work, not its speed. Also not the same as Autonomy. How prescribed the method is says nothing about how novel the output is — a rigid playbook can govern genuinely new work, and a fully self-directed team can spend all of it refining what exists. Do not read “follows a detailed brief” as low Innovation or “builds their own approach” as high Innovation; those are decision-rights facts and belong under Autonomy.

bands.text: The work is making an existing product better rather than creating a new one — incremental improvement to something already in market, no new-category bets.
Mostly improving things that already exist; occasional genuinely new bets at the edges.
Real split between maintaining and creating; no dominant stance.
New-product or new-capability work is common; experimentation encouraged.
R&D-forward, novel products, “0-to-1,” research culture, explicit tolerance for failed experiments.

dimensions.name: Decision Basis
dimensions.measures: What decisions actually rest on — experience, taste and judgement vs. metrics, experiments and analysis.
dimensions.where_to_look: “Data-driven” language, A/B testing and analytics infrastructure, metrics-gated launches, dashboards, KPI- or analytics-heavy job responsibilities, vs. founder-gut, design-led, “trust your judgement,” or “taste and curation” signals. Do NOT count language about approval layers, ownership, independence, or process formality here — that is Autonomy, see keep_distinct.
dimensions.keep_distinct: Score the basis of decisions, not their quality — a taste-led company is not worse than a data-led one, they select for different people. Also not the same as Autonomy: this dimension is about what a decision rests on (data vs. judgement), not who has authority to make it or how much process surrounds it. “Decisively,” “ownership,” “without a formalized process,” “little or no direction,” “following procedures,” and “conservative, long-term view” are Autonomy or values signals, not Decision signals, even when they sit in the same sentence as something that sounds decision-related. A company can require heavy approval and still be entirely data-driven within that approval process, or grant total independence and still run on pure gut feel.

bands.text: Taste, vision and experience lead. Founder gut or design-led; “trust your judgement.”
Judgement-first, data used to confirm rather than decide.

Both judgement and data carry weight depending on the call. Use this band when different parts of the packet point to different poles — that is what it exists for. Do not resolve a genuine conflict in the evidence by picking the quote you find most persuasive; that is exactly the kind of read that produces spread between raters.
Metrics and experiments usually drive decisions; judgement fills gaps.
“Data-driven,” experiment-gated, metrics-first, A/B-everything, analytics-heavy.
